drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: You had the White king pinned in the center, and the killer move was Nd5+ — check from f6, forcing exd5 since the king has no better way to meet it. That opens the e-file for Rfe1+, pushing the king to d6, and then your queen on g7 just grabs the rook with Qxf8+. Instead you took the free pawn with Nxh7, and Black got to breathe: after Rd8 and Qf6+ Ke8, the attack cools off and you gave back over a full pawn of your advantage. When the enemy king is stuck in the middle like that, hunt for the check that keeps him running before you reach for a pawn.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Look at the White king on e2 — it's almost out of squares, and your knight on e6 has a mating shot with Nf4+: after the forced Ke3, your bishop on d5 swings to c5 and it's checkmate right there. Instead you grabbed the pawn with Qxe5+, still check, but White blocks with Ne4; after Bxe4, Qc1, the mate is gone and you just end up castling queenside yourself a few moves later — still winning big, but you traded a forced mate for a long grind. When the enemy king is this boxed in, always look for the check that removes his last escape square before taking a free pawn — mate ends the game on the spot, material doesn't.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king is still stuck on e1, and your queen on f4 has a great route in with Qg3+, forcing Ke2, and then Qxe5+ grabs the e5 pawn with another check, chasing the king to f2 before Qd4+ brings it right back to e2 — you're harvesting material while the king never gets to relax. Retreating the knight to e6 instead let White off the hook: after Qc1 and Ne2, White untangles and you lose the initiative that was worth almost three pawns of advantage. Checks that also grab material are almost always worth more than a quiet developing move — keep the king running while you're ahead.

drills.title: vs kylewms0 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Notice White's bishop on d3 — it sits right on the same file as White's own queen on d1, blocking it from defending the pawn on d4. That means Nxd4 with your f6 knight just wins a clean pawn for free, and the knight lands centrally hitting c2 and e2. Instead you traded on e5 with Nxe5; after fxe5, the pawn recaptures and now attacks your f6 knight too, so you lose a tempo pulling it back and hand White a strong pawn duo on d4/e5 for nothing extra. Before trading a piece, check whether the defender of the square you're eyeing is actually blocked by its own piece — that's free material sitting there.

drills.coachNote: Look at the diagonal from White's queen on d1 straight through e2 and f3 to g4 — it's completely empty, so the instant your knight lands on g4, Qxg4 just wins it for nothing. That's exactly what happens, and instead of real compensation you're left scrambling with ...c5 and ...e5 for pawn play a piece down. The move e5 first does the job properly: after dxe5 hits your knight on f6, only then does Ng4 make sense as the retreat, and Nf3 shows White respecting it instead of just snapping it off. Always check open diagonals to the enemy queen before parking a piece on them — that habit alone saves this knight.

drills.coachNote: You were winning by almost two pawns, but your own king on g8 only has the pawns on g7 and h6 protecting it, and White's bishop on f5 and queen on c2 are both aimed straight at that shelter. Pushing d4 ignores all of that: White plays Be6+, forcing your king to h8, then Qg6 piles onto the weak dark squares and Be4 keeps the attack rolling — your extra material stops mattering while your king gets hunted. Qg5 was the move that actually deals with the danger, meeting Be6+ Kh8 with f4 and trading queens via Qg3+ Qf2, shutting the attack down while you're still clearly winning. When your king's shelter is this thin, defend it before you cash in your advantage elsewhere.

drills.title: vs m76yem (818) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: Your queen on d1 was attacked by the knight on e3, but that knight isn't just forking your queen — it's also guarding g2, and Black's queen on g4 is one move from Qxg2#, mate, because your king on g1 can't recapture past a defended square with no flight squares left. Playing Qe2 solves the small problem — the queen escapes — but ignores the real one, and Black just plays Qxg2#, game over. fxe3 was the move: it captures the knight outright, removes the guard on g2, and kills the mate threat while keeping your big material edge, with Qf5 Nh4 Qxf7 Rxf7 Rxf7 still clearly winning. When a piece attacks you, always ask what else it's doing before you just move out of the way — the bigger threat is often hiding behind the obvious one.

drills.coachNote: Before you grab that pawn, look at who's covering d4 - nobody of yours, but black's rook on a4 sits on the same rank and is watching it the whole time. The move was Rc1-c7, dropping your rook onto the 7th rank first; after Ne3 Nxe3 dxe3 Rxe3 you're the one picking up material, and Ra2 keeps your rook active. Before any capture, scan every enemy rook and pawn sharing a rank, file, or diagonal with the square you're landing on.

Be6 keeps the bishop safe and even lets you trade on your own terms: Bxe6, fxe6, clean and equal. Kf7 first was the fix - tuck the king off the back rank, so when bxa8=Q happens next you simply answer Rxa8 with no check attached, down material but stable instead of hunted. Bf5+ looks active since it's check, but it doesn't defend f4: Black plays e6, kicks the f5 bishop back to c2, and then just takes gxf4 — you're down a full piece for nothing. Nxg5 was the fix — it removes the attacker itself, so after fxg5 Bxg5 the tension is gone and your bishop safely re-lands on g5, eyeing Nf6. When a piece is attacked, checks only help if they actually solve that problem — otherwise you're just stalling the loss.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same issue as before — the g5 pawn already attacks your f4 bishop, so it's falling one way or another; what matters is what you get for it. e4 strikes the center while Black's king is still stuck on d7: gxf4 exd5 hits the c6 knight and rips the position open, with Qa4+ still coming — real compensation. Bf5+ instead spends a tempo on a check that fixes nothing: Black blocks with e6, your bishop retreats to c2, and gxf4 takes it anyway — except now Black just castles and the king is safe. When a piece is lost regardless, pick the version that keeps lines open, not the one that lets your opponent tidy up for free.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Scan the c1-to-g5 diagonal before that knight lands there — it's wide open, nothing on d2, e3, or f4, and White's bishop on c1 is staring straight down it. Ng5 just hangs the piece: Bxg5 wins it outright, and if you try f6 to win the bishop back, Nxe5 grabs your e5 pawn too with tempo, so you're down a full piece for nothing. Nd6 keeps the knight safe while still covering the center; after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 Bg6 the position stays balanced and everything's still on the board. A bishop parked on its home square is easy to forget, but the diagonal doesn't go away — check it before you hop a piece into its path.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g5 is still hanging — White let you off the hook last move by grabbing the e5 pawn instead, but that c1-g5 diagonal is still wide open, and it's on you to fix it now. Be7 doesn't touch the problem: White just plays Bxg5 and wins the knight anyway, then that same bishop keeps marching with Bxe7 next, picking off the bishop you just moved there too. Ne6 was the move — it finally pulls the knight off that diagonal to safety, and after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the game stays roughly level. When a piece is hanging, your next move has to deal with it directly; developing somewhere else doesn't make the threat disappear.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has a clean shot to c7, and from there it hits Black's queen on d8 directly — that's a free tempo sitting on the board. Playing e4 instead lets it slip: Black gets to play Bd7 first, developing the bishop and giving the queen breathing room, so the bite is gone by the time you circle back to Bc7. The point of Bc7 is to keep hassling that queen while Black's pieces are still tangled — Qd7, then b6 cramps the queenside and Nc6/Ra4 build real pressure with Black stuck passive. You were still winning either way, but when a tempo-grabbing shot like that is available, take it immediately before your opponent gets a free move to untangle.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Same theme as last move — Qc5 directly challenges Black's queen on b6, and because Black's pieces are still undeveloped that offer comes with strings: after Qd8, Bd6 hits the f8 rook, Re8 has to defend, and Bxe7 wins you a favorable trade with the knight. Qc3 lets the moment slip again — it challenges nothing, so Black finally gets to play Bd7 with tempo, and by the time you try Qc5 next it's too late: Bxb5 just grabs your pawn since nothing defends it anymore. The pattern across both moves is the same — you had a fast way to keep needling Black's tangled pieces, and each slower move handed over exactly the tempo needed to catch up.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're down material, but your knight on d6 has a lifeline — Nf5+ isn't just check, it's a fork: that same knight hits White's king on g3 and the rook on g7 at once. White has to move the king, say Kf4, and then Nxg7 wins the rook back, putting you right back in the fight. Nb7 throws that away — it threatens nothing and walks straight into Rc7+, forcing your king to d8, after which Rxb7 scoops the knight for free. Whenever a knight can jump into check, get in the habit of asking what else that square hits — a fork like this can flip a losing position, and missing it here sealed the game.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning, but look at the d-file — it's wide open between your rook on d8 and White's rook on d1, nothing in between them. Rd7 walks your rook straight onto that same file, and White simply plays Rxd7 for free — you've handed back a whole rook for nothing. Bxg3+ was the shot instead: your bishop grabs the g3 pawn with check, and after Kxg3 the king is dragged away from defending d1, so Rxd1 wins that rook clean rather than losing your own. Even in a totally winning position, check open files before moving onto them — an open file cuts both ways, and it can just as easily hang your piece as win theirs.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Stop and look at your queen on f3 and the black king stuck on e7 — with your knight on f6 covering d7 and e8, and his own bishop on f8 plus pawns on f7 and e6 jamming every other escape square, that king has nowhere to run. Qxb7+ hits with check along the 7th rank, and after ...Qc7 blocks, Qxc7# is mate — his queen was the only piece that could interpose, and it just gets captured with checkmate. Instead you played exd4, a routine recapture, and let a forced mate in two evaporate into merely 'winning.' When the enemy king's own pieces are jamming its escape squares, hunt for the check that exploits it before doing routine business.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your rook on d1 had a clean shot: Rd7+ is check, and since your knight on f6 already covers d7, his king can't take — the queen on c7 is forced to play Qxd7. Then Nxd7 scoops up his queen for your rook, a trade you should love when you're already up material, and it steers straight into a winning endgame. You played Nd7 instead, forking the rook on b8 and bishop on f8, but he simply saves the bishop with ...Bg7 and the rook with ...Rbc8 over the next couple moves, and the fork fizzles into nothing. A check that forces a specific recapture beats a fork he can wriggle out of.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before playing Qh4, look at the diagonal from e7 to h4 — his queen sits right on it, e7-f6-g5-h4 wide open, and nothing of yours guards h4. So Qxh4 just wins your queen outright, on top of a position where you were already down close to four and a half pawns. One hanging square ends the game right there. Qa3 tucks the queen somewhere safe and useful instead, and you keep fighting with ...Re8, c4, and pushing g4 for kingside space — not winning, but still a game. Before moving your queen anywhere, check what diagonals and files the enemy queen already commands.

drills.explanation: Your e5 pawn was attacked by the d6 pawn; exd6 resolves it cleanly, and after cxd6 you develop normally with Nc3 and Nf3, dead level. Pushing e6 instead placed the pawn on a square Black's f7 pawn covers: fxe6 ate it for free, and after Bd3 Nf6 c4 you were simply a pawn down out of the opening.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your pawn on e5 had a clean option: exd6, just taking his pawn on d6, and after ...cxd6 you get to plant a knight on e5 with Nc3 and Ne5 — a great outpost hitting c6 and f7 while his knight on d7 is still tangled up. Instead you pushed e6, but that pawn is defended by nobody — his f7 pawn just takes it, fxe6, and you've handed him a free pawn and a strong center for nothing. Before pushing a pawn forward, always ask who's actually defending the square it lands on; e6 was covered by exactly no one.

drills.explanation: Your queen on e5 was attacked by the knight on f3, and Qe6 was the safe square — it stays active and out of reach, and if Nd4 chases it again, Qe5 returns with White having nothing better than repeating. Qd6 stepped onto the open d-file instead: Rad1 hit the queen with your own rook on d8 lined up behind it, and after Qb4, Rxd8+ Bxd8 handed White the file and the initiative.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: Watch the d-file: the moment you play Qd6, your queen sits directly in front of your own rook on d8, and Rad1 lines his rook straight up against both. Your queen has to run with ...Qb4, and once it does, Rxd8+ trades into your rook with check, forcing ...Bxd8 — you've been shoved off the file and lost the initiative in a position that was dead equal, a 3.6 pawn swing for nothing. Qe6 keeps your queen off that file entirely and supports your knight jumping to d4, hitting his queen on c2. Before parking your queen on a file your own rook occupies, check whether he can pile a rook onto it.

drills.explanation: Bxb4 just takes a free pawn — the whole point of testing the Polish. White regains it with Bxe5, but after Nf6, c3, Be7 you've swapped his wing pawn for your e-pawn and developed smoothly. Nc6 guarded e5 but walked into b5: the knight had to retreat to e7, and Bxe5 took the pawn anyway — White kept his extra pawn and gained time.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: After 2.Bb2, look at his b4 pawn — the bishop that used to guard it just left c1, and nothing else covers b4, so your f8 bishop can simply take it, Bxb4, for free. You played Nc6 instead, developing but ignoring the freebie, and now b5 hits your knight, kicking it to e7 where it no longer guards your own e5 pawn — so Bxe5 grabs that one right back, and the edge you could've banked slips over to him instead. When you spot an undefended pawn sitting there, grab it before developing, because a tempo-losing retreat can hand the material right back.

drills.explanation: Nd4 does everything at once: it saves the knight from the d5 pawn and attacks White's queen on f3, winning a free tempo. After Qd1 you follow with Bf5 and b5, developing with real energy. Nce7 retreated to a passive square that blocks your own f8 bishop, and gave White time for d4, building a big centre unchallenged.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c6 is under attack from the pawn on d5, so it has to move — but where matters. Nd4 solves the problem and does more: it steps out of the pawn's reach and lands on his queen on f3, forcing it back to d1, and you follow up actively with ...Bf5 and ...b5, hitting his bishop on c4. You played Nce7 instead, a purely defensive retreat that blocks in your own f8 bishop and just hands White a free tempo to keep developing. When a piece is attacked, look for the retreat square that also throws out a threat, not just the safest one.

drills.explanation: Kb6 steps to safety, and play stays balanced: Rh5 Rg8, then Rxf5 for him and Rxg3 for you — an even pawn-grab. Kd6 walked onto exactly the square the knight on e5 forks from f7: Nf7+ hits king and rook together, and Ke7 Nxd8 Kxd8 costs you a rook for a knight. From e5, f7 was the springboard covering both d6 and d8.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your king on c7 needs to step off the knight's radar, and c7-d6 doesn't do that — Nf7+ forks you, the knight jumping from e5 to f7 with check, hitting both your king and the rook on d8. You have to move again, and Nxd8+ just scoops the rook, Kxd8 recaptures the knight, but you've dropped the exchange in a position that was already lost. Kb6 sidesteps the whole fork, tucking the king somewhere no knight check can reach, and keeps your rook on d8 alive so you can fight for pawns with ...Rg8 and ...Rxg3. Whenever a knight's nearby, check every square it can jump to with check before you move your king.

drills.explanation: The e5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxe5 turns the threat around: it wins the pawn, and after Nxe5 Bxe5 your bishop sits beautifully in the center eyeing g7, leaving Black scrambling with Qg6 before you castle and meet Bf5 calmly. Castling first simply dropped the bishop — exf4 took it for free, and you were a piece down by move nine.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: Before you castle, look at the tension: Black's pawn on e5 is attacking your bishop on f4, while your bishop on d3 is attacking Black's knight on e4 - both sides have a piece hanging. Nxe5 cashes in first: after Nxe5 Nxe5 Bxe5 you land a pawn up with a monster bishop on e5, and Qg6 O-O Bf5 keeps you comfortable. Instead O-O ignores the threat entirely, so Black just plays exf4 and your bishop is gone for free - that's the whole +1.6-to-losing swing. Whenever two pieces are mutually attacking each other, resolve it before you spend a move elsewhere.

drills.explanation: Qg4 stepped straight onto the c8-bishop's open diagonal — c8 to g4 had nothing in the way, and Bxg4 took the queen; after h3, Be6 the bishop went home and Black was simply up material. Qh5 was the safe square, or better yet Nd2 first: develop the stranded b1 knight, tuck the queen on e1, and Nf3 finally challenges the bishop on g5.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: Before playing Qg4, trace the diagonal your queen is walking onto: Black's other bishop, still parked on c8, has a wide-open road down c8-d7-e6-f5-g4, and your queen lands right at the end of it. Bxg4 simply wins your queen for a bishop, on top of a position that was already lost at -4.0. Qh5 avoids that diagonal completely while still attacking the bishop on g5, forcing Be7, and after Nd2 Be6 Rxf4 you actually win back the f4 pawn and get some fight left. Before any queen move, check every open diagonal and file aimed at that square - that's exactly how this one got lost.

drills.explanation: Both Black bishops were loose — f5 to your bishop on d3, g5 to your knight — but capture order decided everything. Bxf5 takes the one with a counter-capture available, since the f5 bishop and your d3 bishop attack each other; after gxf5, Nd4 centralizes powerfully. Nxg5 allowed the in-between move Bxd3, and after Qxd3 Qxg5 Black had won the piece right back.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Nxg5 grabs a bishop, but your own bishop on d3 and Black's bishop on f5 are eyeing each other on that same diagonal - after Nxg5 Bxd3 Qxd3 Qxg5, Black takes your knight right back, so the piece you thought you won just walks off the board while Black's queen and the f4 pawn roll toward your king. Bxf5 wins that same exchange on your terms instead: it removes Black's active bishop first, and after gxf5 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 h4 the position settles with material even and your king safe. Before grabbing a piece, always check whether your own piece is hanging on that very same move.

drills.explanation: Bxf5 resolves the bishop standoff your way: after Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5 you have Bd7 — the bishop lands in Black's camp hitting the knight on c6 and the rook on e8. dxe5 handed Black the move order: Bxg5 came first, and after Bxf5 gxf5 Nd4 the trades fizzled — about a pawn and a half lost purely to capturing in the wrong sequence.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: dxe5 looks like a free pawn, but it gives up the one thing holding the center together: your pawn on d4 was the only thing stopping Black's knight from landing on d4 forever. After dxe5 Bxg5 Bxf5 gxf5, Black plays Nd4 and that knight just sits there unkickable, dominating the board. Bxf5 was the move to play first instead - trade off Black's active bishop while the tension's still there, and after Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5 Bd7 Reb8 the position stays level with nothing hanging. When a pawn is the only thing keeping an enemy piece off a great square, think twice before trading it away.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a8 had the bishop on c8 pinned against the queen on d8, and Rfc1 — either rook works, but the f1 rook keeps a1 at home — piles onto it down the fully open c-file. Black's best is to bail out with Be6, when Qxd8+ Nxd8 trades into a pleasant endgame for you. g3 let the moment slip: d5 and then Nd6 covered c8, and the target wriggled free.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're completely winning at +6.3 with your queen sitting deep on a8, but g3 is a slow, do-nothing move that hands Black a free tempo. Rfc1 was right instead - it activates your rook on the c-file, and after Be6 Qxd8+ Nxd8 d5 Bxd5 you trade queens and simplify into a cleanly won endgame while still up material. g3 instead lets Black play d5 and reroute the knight to d6, attacking your queen on a8 directly and costing you time to untangle - that's how +6.3 slips to +4.3. Even in a totally winning position, keep activating your worst piece instead of playing a safe waiting move.

drills.explanation: Nxe4 wins the e4 pawn cleanly — d5 can't recapture, because that would open the b3–g8 diagonal from your queen straight onto Black's king. After f5 the knight slides back to g3, and c4 starts prying at d5 next. Nh2 retreated for nothing: f5 cemented Black's pawn on e4, and you had to play f3 to challenge it anyway, a tempo and a pawn poorer.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's pawn on e4 pushed forward without real support, and your knight on d2 can simply eat it with Nxe4 - a clean pawn plus a cleared center. Instead Nh2 tucks your knight onto the rim doing nothing, so Black keeps building with f5, then the dangerous f3, wedging a pawn right next to your own king, with Re8 and c4 following - that's the 1.5-pawn swing from a comfortable +1.1 toward equal. Notice that in the real line Black doesn't even bother recapturing dxe4 after Nxe4 - you're just up a full pawn outright. Before shuffling a piece to a passive square, check first whether there's a hanging pawn to simply take.
